FOR INDEPENDENT STAFFING AGENCIES AND RECRUITERS

A 45% markup is not a 45% margin. It is not a 31% one either.

You mark up the pay rate, so the markup has to carry the whole employer burden before a cent of it is profit — FICA, federal and state unemployment, the comp code the work falls under, PTO, benefits, screening, and the six weeks you fund payroll before the client pays. Put a real placement in below and see the bill rate, the burden an hour, the margin the markup actually earns, and the markup your target margin needs.

Markup vs. margin in staffing — why the usual conversion is wrong here

This calculator vs. TempWorks — what each tool is actually for

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet — why markup / (1 + markup) overstates the real margin

Employee vs. contractor cost calculator — the same employer-burden math, for a business staffing a role itself rather than billing a client for a placement

The placement

The pay rate and the markup you would quote. Everything below prices this one assignment.

Employer burden

These are your own figures. SUTA comes off your state rate notice, the comp rate off your policy declarations for the class code this job falls under. The defaults are a plausible light-industrial placement, not a recommendation.

Getting paid

You fund payroll weekly and collect later. This is what that gap costs, and what you hold back for invoices that never land.

A shareable link carries your own pay rate, markup, burden rates and payment terms — treat one like your rate sheet. It is built in your browser and never sent to a server; send it to a partner reviewing the same placement, not to the client. Your last placement is also saved in this browser so it is here next time you open the page; “Start a fresh placement” clears it.

Where the burden goes

      Common questions

      Is a 45% markup a 45% gross margin?

      No, and the gap is larger than the usual correction. Converting markup to margin the textbook way gives 45/145 = 31%, and that conversion is only right when the number you marked up is the whole cost. In staffing you mark up the pay rate, and every dollar of FICA, unemployment tax, workers’ compensation, PTO and benefits sits outside it. On the worked example — $22 an hour, a 3% SUTA on a $12,000 base, a $6.20 per $100 comp code, collected on net-45 — a 45% markup returns a 15.8% gross margin, not 31%. Hitting 20% would take a 52.6% markup.

      Why is a short assignment more expensive per hour?

      Because FUTA and SUTA are charged on a wage base, not on every dollar. FUTA applies to the first $7,000 a worker earns in the year and your state’s unemployment tax to the first (commonly) $7,000 to $60,000. A worker who bills 420 hours pays almost the entire annual charge inside those 420 hours; the same worker on a 2,000-hour assignment spreads it over five times as many. This calculator charges the capped amount rather than a flat percentage, so the effect appears on its own and a 12-week placement prices differently from a year-long one without you doing anything.

      What is the break-even markup?

      The markup at which the placement finishes exactly level: burden covered, payroll funded, bad debt reserved, and nothing left. On the worked example it is 21.9%. It is worth knowing because it is the floor a negotiation can reach and not the number to quote — the distance between it and your markup is the entire profit on the placement, which is why shaving five points off a quote is a large fraction of the margin rather than a small fraction of the price.

      Why does it charge me for the client’s payment terms?

      Because you pay the worker weekly and the client pays you on net-30, net-45 or later. That money is out the door in the meantime, whether it is financed, factored, or simply your own cash not doing something else. The calculator applies your cost of capital to the loaded cost — the money actually spent, not the invoice — across the days you wait. On the worked example, net-45 at 12% costs $202 of a $2,626 profit. It is the line most markup quotes leave out entirely, and it is the one that turns a thin placement into a losing one.

      How should I bill overtime?

      You pay overtime at 1.5 times the pay rate, so a bill rate that does not also rise by 1.5 earns less margin on every overtime hour and can earn none. Set the two multipliers separately here and see it. One nuance the calculator handles: most states rate workers’ compensation on straight-time-equivalent payroll, so the half-time premium on an overtime hour is excluded from the comp payroll. Leave that box ticked unless your state does not allow the exclusion — it is a real saving on an assignment running heavy overtime, and over-reserving for it prices you out of work you could win.

      Where do I find my SUTA rate and workers’ comp rate?

      Your SUTA rate and wage base are on the annual rate notice your state unemployment agency sends you; the rate is experience-rated, so it is yours and not a national figure. Your workers’ compensation rate is on your policy declarations, quoted per $100 of payroll and set by the class code the work falls under — which is why a clerical placement and a light-industrial placement in the same office are different businesses. The defaults here are illustrative starting points, not advice about which class code applies to a job.

      Is any of this uploaded?

      No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. Your pay rates, markups, comp rate and the margins it works out are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

      Is this legal, tax, or insurance advice?

      No. It is arithmetic on the figures you type. It makes no determination about worker classification, which workers’ compensation class code applies, co-employment, overtime exemption, or your obligations under any state or federal law, and the rates and wage bases it starts with are illustrative and change every year. Check every figure against your own rate notices, policy declarations and payroll records, and against a qualified professional, before you quote a client from it.

      No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, or employment advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, which workers’ compensation class code applies to a job, whether anyone is an employee or a contractor, or what any state or federal law requires of you. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, and the rates and wage bases it starts with are illustrative and change every year. Verify every figure against your own state rate notice, policy declarations, and payroll records, and against a qualified professional, before quoting a client from it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

      Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. Your pay rates, markups, comp rate and the margins worked out here are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count — those are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and switched off automatically for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control. “Copy shareable link” puts the same numbers in the page’s URL fragment instead of a server, and your last placement is saved to this browser’s own local storage so it is here on your next visit — nothing about it leaves your device either way, but whoever holds a link you send can read it.

      Working out what an hour costs your own shop rather than a placement’s? The shop rate calculator does the same job for trade crews, and the certified payroll calculator covers prevailing-wage fringe. Paying yourself instead of a worker? Try the freelance retainer calculator.

      Free and open source. If it changes what you quote, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

markup-vs-margin.html.text:
STAFFING MARKUP CALCULATOR

Markup vs. margin in staffing

Everybody in the trade knows markup and margin are different numbers. Far fewer know that the standard conversion between them — the one every business-school page gives — is wrong for staffing specifically, and wrong in the direction that costs you money.

Price a real placement →

The conversion everyone uses

Markup is added to a cost. Margin is a share of a price. Convert one to the other with markup ÷ (1 + markup), so a 45% markup is a 31% margin. That identity is exactly right — when the thing you marked up is your whole cost.

In staffing it never is. You mark up the pay rate. The pay rate is what the worker receives; it is not what the placement costs you. Everything else you owe on that worker sits outside the number you multiplied.

What sits outside the markup

Take a $22-an-hour light-industrial placement, 40 hours a week for 13 weeks — 520 hours and $11,440 of wages.

CostHow it is chargedOn this placement
FICA7.65% of wages$875
FUTA0.6% of the first $7,000$42
SUTA3% of the first $12,000$343
Workers’ comp$6.20 per $100 of payroll$709
Screening and onboardingonce, per placement$85
Payroll, ATS, admin$0.35 an hour$182
Employer burdenrows rounded to the dollar$2,237

That is $4.30 an hour on top of the $22 wage — a 19.6% burden. So the loaded cost is $26.30 an hour, against a bill rate of $22 × 1.45 = $31.90.

What the 45% actually earns

Across the assignment: $16,588 billed, $13,677 of loaded cost, $202 to fund payroll for the 45 days before the client pays, and $83 held back against invoices that never land. Gross profit $2,626, which on $16,588 of billings is a 15.8% gross margin.

FigureValue
Margin the markup implies (45 ÷ 145)31.0%
Margin the placement earns15.8%
Markup that just breaks even21.9%
Markup needed for a 20% margin52.6%

A recruiter quoting 45% and reporting a 31% margin to an owner is off by nearly half. And the 45% widely repeated as a healthy staffing markup does not reach a 20% gross margin on this placement — it takes 52.6%.

Why one house markup cannot be right

Two inputs move the answer more than anything else, and neither is a national figure:

  • Your workers’ comp rate, quoted per $100 of payroll and set by the class code the work falls under. Clerical codes sit near $1; roofing and framing codes reach $12 and beyond. At the same markup, one of those placements is a business and the other is a favour.
  • Your SUTA rate and wage base, which are experience-rated and set by your state. Wage bases run from about $7,000 to over $60,000, so the same rate charges very different amounts.

A single desk-wide markup applied across a mixed book takes the profit from the light codes and spends it on the heavy ones. That is invisible in a monthly P&L because the two net out; it is only visible per placement.

And short assignments are the expensive ones

FUTA and SUTA are charged on a wage base, not proportionally. The example above pays $11,440 of wages, which is past the $7,000 FUTA base and most of the way through a $12,000 SUTA base — so it carries $385 of the annual charge inside 13 weeks. Run the same worker a full year and the charge rises only to $402 — 4% more money spread over four times the hours. Per hour that is 74¢ against 19¢: the seasonal placement costs nearly four times as much in unemployment tax as the annual one, and no markup rule of thumb sees it.

Put your own rates in →

The short version

  • Markup is on the pay rate. Margin is on the invoice. They convert — but not with the textbook identity, because burden sits outside the markup.
  • Your break-even markup is a number worth knowing and not a number to quote. The gap between it and your markup is the entire profit.
  • Price the comp code and the term, not the desk average.
  • Count the days you wait to be paid. It is real money and it is nobody’s line item.

Common questions

What is the difference between markup and margin in staffing?

Markup is added to the pay rate: a 45% markup on $22 bills $31.90. Margin is a share of the invoice: gross profit divided by what you billed. They are different denominators, so they are never the same number. The textbook conversion is markup / (1 + markup) — 45/145 = 31% — but that only holds when the figure you marked up is the whole cost, and in staffing it is not.

Why is the usual markup-to-margin conversion wrong in staffing?

Because you mark up the pay rate, and the pay rate is not your cost. FICA, federal and state unemployment tax, workers’ compensation, PTO accrual, benefits, screening and payroll admin all sit outside the number you marked up. On a $22 light-industrial placement those add about $4.30 an hour, so the loaded cost is $26.30 against a $31.90 bill rate. The gross margin is 15.8%, not the 31% the conversion suggests.

What markup do I need for a 20% gross margin?

It depends entirely on your burden, which is why no published figure answers it. On the worked example here — $22 an hour, 3% SUTA on a $12,000 base, a $6.20 per $100 comp code, net-45 terms at a 12% cost of capital — a 20% gross margin needs a 52.6% markup, not the 45% commonly quoted as healthy. Change the comp code and that number moves several points on its own.

Does the same markup earn the same margin on every placement?

No, and this is the expensive part. Workers’ compensation is quoted per $100 of payroll by class code, so a clerical placement near $1 and a roofing placement near $12 carry very different burdens at the identical markup. State unemployment rates are experience-rated and their wage bases range from about $7,000 to over $60,000. A single house markup applied across a mixed desk quietly subsidises the heavy codes out of the light ones.

Why does a short assignment cost more per hour?

FUTA and SUTA are charged on a wage base rather than on every dollar. FUTA applies to a worker’s first $7,000 of wages in the year and state unemployment to the first (commonly) $7,000 to $60,000. A 420-hour seasonal placement pays nearly the whole annual charge inside those 420 hours, while a 2,000-hour one spreads it across five times as many. Per hour, the short assignment is the expensive one.

Should I count the cost of waiting for the client to pay?

Yes. You pay the worker weekly and the client pays on net-30, net-45 or later, so the loaded cost is out of your account for the whole gap — financed, factored, or simply your own cash sitting still. On the worked example, net-45 at a 12% cost of capital takes $202 out of a $2,626 gross profit. It is left out of nearly every markup quote, and on a thin placement it is the difference between a profit and a loss.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, or employment advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, which workers’ compensation class code applies to a job, whether anyone is an employee or a contractor, or what any state or federal law requires of you. The rates and wage bases used in the worked example are illustrative and change every year. Verify every figure against your own state rate notice, policy declarations, and payroll records, and against a qualified professional, before quoting a client from it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator runs entirely on your device — no account, no network requests, and no figure you type is ever uploaded.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Staffing markup calculator

Staffing markup calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet can price a placement's real margin correctly. It has to carry a formula for every burden line, cap FUTA and SUTA at their wage base by hand, and get rebuilt correctly every time a rate or a comp code changes -- or it quietly reports markup / (1 + markup) instead, which is only right when the pay rate is the whole cost.

Price a real placement →

A spreadsheet is how most independent agencies price a placement today, and there is nothing wrong with the arithmetic itself: markup on the pay rate, burden as a percentage, margin as a formula. The formula most desks actually use is markup / (1 + markup) — 45% markup becomes a 31% margin — and that identity is exactly right when the number being marked up is the whole cost of the placement. It isn't. FICA, federal and state unemployment tax, workers' compensation, PTO accrual, benefits, onboarding and payroll admin all sit outside the pay rate, and a one-line formula has no way to know that.

This calculator prices the loaded cost directly: it charges FUTA and SUTA against their wage base rather than as a flat percentage, so a short assignment carries the effect on its own; it applies the workers' comp class rate to the comp-eligible payroll, excluding the overtime premium where the state allows it; and it prices the cost of funding payroll for the days between paying workers weekly and collecting the invoice on the client's actual terms. It reports the real gross margin next to the margin the markup implies, and the break-even and target-margin markups directly — no formula to write or re-check.

What each one gets right, and what it costs to get there.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Can a spreadsheet price a placement's real gross margin? Yes — if it caps FUTA and SUTA at the wage base, excludes the OT premium from comp payroll where allowed, and prices the cost of the client's payment terms, all correctly and every time a rate changes.
Is markup / (1 + markup) the real margin? Only when the pay rate is the whole cost. In staffing it isn't — that is the gap this calculator prices.
What markup hits a 20% gross margin on this comp code and these terms? This calculator's target-margin markup, computed instantly, plus a markup ladder for negotiating a discount.
Is anything typed in uploaded anywhere? No. Neither a spreadsheet nor this calculator sends a placement's numbers anywhere; this calculator runs entirely in your browser.

Nothing here says a spreadsheet formula is wrong to use — a correctly built one prices a placement exactly as well as this calculator does. The difference is what it costs to get there: this calculator applies the same wage-base-capped, comp-payroll- excluded, payment-term-priced method every time, with no formula to write, copy down a column, or re-check after a rate changes.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet price a staffing placement's real margin?

It can, but the one-line formula most desks use — markup / (1 + markup) — only gives the real gross margin when the pay rate is the whole cost being marked up. In staffing it isn't: FICA, FUTA, SUTA, workers' comp, PTO, benefits, onboarding and payroll admin all sit outside the pay rate and inside the real cost. A spreadsheet can price that correctly too, but it has to carry a formula for each of those lines, including capping FUTA and SUTA at their wage bases rather than charging them as a flat percentage, and that formula has to be rebuilt correctly every time a rate, a comp code, or a state changes.

Why does the usual markup-to-margin formula overstate the real margin?

Because it assumes the pay rate is the only cost in the placement. Employer burden — FICA, unemployment tax, workers' comp, PTO accrual, benefits, screening and payroll admin — is real cost that sits outside the pay rate, so it is invisible to markup / (1 + markup) entirely. A 45% markup implies a 31% margin by that formula; once burden, the cost of funding payroll on the client's terms, and bad debt are counted, the placement can earn well under half of that, or lose money outright on a heavy workers' comp class code.

What does a hand-built spreadsheet have to get right that this calculator does automatically?

Three things that are each easy to get wrong once and never notice: charging FUTA and SUTA against their wage base with min(wages, wageBase) rather than as a flat percentage on every dollar, so a short assignment doesn't silently overcharge or undercharge the unemployment line; excluding the overtime premium from workers' comp payroll where the state allows it, rather than charging comp on the full 1.5x wage; and pricing the cost of funding payroll for the days between paying workers weekly and collecting the invoice on the client's actual terms, which a markup-only sheet usually omits altogether.

Is this page affiliated with any spreadsheet software?

No. This page names no specific spreadsheet product — Excel, Google Sheets, or otherwise — and compares against the practice of pricing a placement in a spreadsheet formula generally, not any one tool.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.

Open the staffing markup calculator to price your own placement, or read why markup and margin are not the same number in staffing.

vs-tempworks.html.text:
← Staffing markup calculator

Staffing markup calculator vs. TempWorks

Different jobs: one prices a single placement in your browser right now; the other runs an agency's whole front and back office as a paid subscription.

Price a real placement →

TempWorks is a well-known staffing agency software suite, described on its own site (tempworks.com) as covering applicant tracking, CRM, timekeeping, payroll processing, invoicing, tax compliance and reporting for staffing and recruiting firms. It is the kind of system an agency runs its whole desk on once it has clients, workers, and payroll cycles to manage continuously — onboarded, configured with the agency's own rates and terms, and paid for every month it runs.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This calculator has no account, no client records, no payroll run, and nothing to configure ahead of time. It exists for the narrower question that comes up dozens of times a week on a staffing desk, often while someone is still on the phone with a client: given this pay rate and this markup, what does the placement actually earn once employer burden, funding the payroll, and bad debt are all counted — and what markup does it need to hit a real target margin?

What each tool answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What does this one placement's markup actually earn once FICA, FUTA, SUTA, workers' comp, PTO, benefits and payment terms are counted? This calculator — it prices the placement from numbers you already have on a rate notice and policy declaration, with no setup.
Run my agency's applicant tracking, client CRM, timekeeping, payroll and invoicing day to day? TempWorks or a comparable paid platform — ongoing operations across many workers and clients are a job this page does not attempt.
What markup do I need to quote right now to hit a 20% gross margin on this specific comp code and term? This calculator — the break-even markup and target-margin markup are computed instantly from the figures you type, with a markup ladder for negotiating a discount.
Keep a system of record for placements, timesheets and pay runs across the whole desk? TempWorks or a comparable paid platform — this page remembers nothing between visits except what your own browser stores locally, and makes no claim to be a system of record.

This calculator is deliberately the opposite shape from an agency-wide platform: nothing to configure, nothing billed monthly, and nothing typed here ever leaves your browser. That makes it a fast, honest gut-check on one quote — not a competitor to the operational system an agency runs its business on, which is exactly the job a platform like TempWorks is built for.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. TempWorks prices its software by quote rather than publishing a rate card, so no dollar figure for it is stated here — only its well-documented category and feature set.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or a platform like TempWorks?

They serve different needs and most agencies that adopt a platform still reach for a quick standalone calculator when pricing one placement on the phone. TempWorks is a paid, all-in-one staffing agency software suite — applicant tracking, CRM, timekeeping, payroll processing, invoicing and reporting — built to run an agency's ongoing operations end to end, described on its own site. Getting a number out of a system like that means it is already configured with your burden rates, tax setup and client terms, which takes onboarding and an active subscription. This calculator needs none of that: type a pay rate, a markup, your SUTA and workers' comp rate, and your payment terms, and it shows the loaded cost, the real gross margin behind the markup, the break-even markup, and the markup a target margin needs — in your browser, with no account, in the time it takes to load the page.

Is this page affiliated with TempWorks?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by TempWorks Software, Inc. TempWorks is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
